passages.t: The LORD fights, and living water flows
passages.happening:
‘Behold, a day of the LORD is coming when your plunder will be divided in your presence’ (verse 1). God will gather the nations against Jerusalem; the city will be taken, its houses looted, and half its people taken into exile (verse 2). The verse names the violence done to the women of the city; these notes name it as the crime it is and do not describe it.

‘Then the LORD will go out to fight against those nations, as He fights in the day of battle’ (verse 3). His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem, and it will split in two, forming a great valley through which the people flee, as they fled from the earthquake in the days of Uzziah (verses 4-5). There will be no light or cold, a day known only to the LORD, and at evening there will be light (verses 6-7). ‘And on that day living water will flow out from Jerusalem, half of it toward the Eastern Sea and the other half toward the Western Sea, in summer and winter alike’ (verse 8). ‘On that day the LORD will become King over all the earth’ (verse 9). The land around will be leveled and Jerusalem raised up, and it will live securely (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
The last chapter gathers the book's hopes into one picture. Jerusalem falls, and then God himself fights for it. The Mount of Olives lies just east of the city across the Kidron valley; here it splits, opening a way of escape. The earthquake in Uzziah's day was remembered for centuries.

Living water means running, fresh water, not water stored in a cistern. Here water flows from the city east to the Dead Sea and west to the Mediterranean, in the dry summer as well as the wet winter. Ezekiel saw the same river from the temple.

Verse 9 is the heart of the chapter: the LORD alone will be king over all the earth, and his name the only name.
passages.later: Amos dated his words to ‘two years before the earthquake’ (Amos 1:1). Ezekiel saw water flowing from under the temple toward the east (Ezekiel 47:1).
passages.hard:
Is this chapter a literal prediction of a future battle, and how should its violence against the nations be read?

Christians read the chapter in different ways, and this site takes no side. Many dispensational and other premillennial interpreters take it as a prediction of real future events: a final siege of Jerusalem, Christ's return to the Mount of Olives, and his reign on earth, during which the nations literally keep the Feast of Tabernacles. Many amillennial and other interpreters read it as prophetic imagery drawn from Israel's world, the temple, the feasts and the enemy nations, to describe the triumph of God's kingdom, fulfilled in Christ, the gathering of the nations into the church, and the new creation. Others take a middle path, seeing a present fulfillment and a future completion.

On any reading, the fighting is God's, and the chapter gives no warrant for violence against any people. It makes no claim about any modern state, city or border.

A word for anyone who has been sexually assaulted. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The chapter's center is that the LORD will be king over all the earth. Ask what it would mean for him to be king over all of your life. And ask where you need living water to flow into a dry place.

passages.t: The nations worship, and everything is holy
passages.happening:
The LORD will strike the peoples who warred against Jerusalem with a plague and with panic, so that they turn on one another (verses 12-13). The verses describe the plague in harsh terms, which these notes do not repeat. Judah too will fight, and the wealth of the nations will be gathered, and the plague will strike their animals as well (verses 14-15).

Then the survivors of the nations will go up year after year to worship the King, the LORD of Hosts, and to keep the Feast of Tabernacles (verse 16). Any families that do not go up will have no rain (verses 17-19). ‘On that day, HOLY TO THE LORD will be inscribed on the bells of the horses’ (verse 20), and the cooking pots in the LORD's house will be like the sacred bowls before the altar. Every pot in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy to the LORD, and there will no longer be a Canaanite, a trader, in the house of the LORD (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The Feast of Tabernacles was the autumn harvest festival, when Israel lived in shelters to remember the wilderness and gave thanks for the year's crops. The nations who once attacked Jerusalem now come to keep Israel's feast. Withholding rain fits the feast, which celebrated the harvest the rains brought.

Holy to the LORD was engraved on the gold plate of the high priest's turban. Now it is written on the bells of horses, and ordinary cooking pots become as holy as the vessels of the altar. The holiness of the temple spills out into the whole of life.

The last line can be read as no Canaanite or as no trader, since the word meant both; either way, the temple will no longer be a place of profit or of what does not belong to God.
passages.later: The high priest's turban bore a gold plate engraved ‘HOLY TO THE LORD’ (Exodus 28:36). The law set out the Feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:39-43).
passages.asks: The book ends with bells and cooking pots made holy. Ask what ordinary parts of your life you have kept separate from God. And ask what it would look like for them to be holy to the LORD.
